meta.title: Prior knowledge-informed centroiding CNN for planetary and small bodies navigation
meta.authorsHtml: Umberto Mondini<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Pietro Califano<sup>1</sup>, Paolo Panicucci<sup>1</sup>, Francesco Topputo<sup>1</sup>

abstract: This work proposes a prior-informed convolutional neural network for centroid estimation in autonomous optical navigation around planetary and small bodies. The architecture integrates an EfficientNet backbone with handcrafted image descriptors and physical priors through a Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) conditioning module, predicting a correction to the intensity-weighted center of brightness rather than the center of figure directly. Centroiding for non-spherical targets is challenging due to irregular geometries, strong self-shadowing, large phase angles, and partial field-of-view coverage. Existing deep learning approaches have demonstrated improved robustness to illumination variability but typically generalize poorly across different body shapes. The proposed model is compared against two algorithms developed for the RAMSES’ Farinella CubeSat mission: an analytical COB correction law and a lightweight handcrafted-feature network. Evaluation covers training targets (Itokawa and Bennu) and unseen bodies (Apophis, Mars, Moon). The FiLM model consistently achieves the lowest centroiding errors and best generalization across all test scenarios. Inference on a NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano runs below 55 ms in the ONNX Runtime framework with CUDA acceleration.

blocks.html: Autonomous optical navigation is essential for planetary and small-body missions operating in close proximity to irregular targets such as Itokawa or Apophis. Estimating the line-of-sight (LoS) direction to the observed body provides direct information on the spacecraft position relative to the target and is therefore fundamental for orbit determination. A computationally efficient solution consists in estimating this direction from images of the target, a task known as centroiding. However, centroiding for non-spherical bodies is challenging: irregular geometries, strong self-shadowing, large phase angles, and partial fieldof-view coverage introduce systematic biases between the estimated centroid and the center of figure (COF), defined as the image projection of the center of mass (COM) under the assumption of uniform density. Classical centroiding approaches include intensity-weighted center of brightness (COB) estimation [1], limb fitting [2], and template correlation with synthetic projections [3]. These methods perform well for near-spherical bodies under moderate illumination but degrade for irregular shapes. Recent work has explored deep learning approaches that directly regress geometric quantities from images [4–6]. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can learn nonlinear mappings from image content to measurements and show improved robustness to illumination variability compared with classical techniques [7]. However, existing learning-based approaches are often tailored to specific target shapes [7, 8], or are evaluated only in limited scenarios. This implies poor generalization to unseen targets. To the authors’ knowledge, no prior work combines CNN feature extraction with explicit physical priors, which could improve generalization across different bodies by exploiting ancillary information routinely available during close-proximity operations.

This work proposes a prior-informed CNN for centroid estimation in planetary and small-body navigation. The model combines convolutional features, handcrafted image descriptors, and physical priors within a unified framework. Image features extracted by an EfficientNet backbone are conditioned through a Feature-wise Linear Modulation module [9], while handcrafted descriptors are incorporated in the regression head. Inspired by residual learning [10], the network predicts a correction to the intensity-weighted COB rather than the COF directly. The proposed model, referred to as the “FiLM" model, is compared with two alternative approaches: a Lommel–Seeliger analytical correction of COB (ACOB) and a lightweight neural model based on handcrafted features (NeuralCOB), both originally developed for the RAMSES’ Farinella CubeSat mission to study asteroid Apophis [11, 12]. The evaluation considers datasets with randomly generated poses and illumination conditions, including image errors and prior uncertainties. Three previously unseen targets representative of bodies of interest for future missions are analyzed: Apophis, Mars, and the Moon. Finally, inference times are measured by running the exported ONNX models on a NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano.

blocks.html: ordinates (u, v) ∈R2. The center of figure, cCOF, is defined as the projection of the body’s center of mass onto the image plane. Any centroiding algorithm can be expressed as a function ˆcCOF = f(I, p), where p is a vector of method-specific inputs. The centroiding error is e = ˆcCOF −cCOF whose empirical statistics and Euclidean norm ∥e∥2 can be used for algorithms evaluation.

Raw grayscale images are first preprocessed to mitigate sensor noise and optical artifacts. The image is binarized using an adaptive threshold equal to the 85th percentile of non-zero pixel intensities, producing a binary mask M ∈{0, 1}H×W . A morphological opening with a 3 × 3 structuring element removes small isolated blobs. The COB and all handcrafted quantities are then computed from the masked image I ⊙M. The handcrafted features include the COB itself, the bounding box of the largest connected component b = [x, y, w, h]⊤, and eight brightness moments (M00, µ20, µ02, µ11, Sx, Sy, Kx, Ky) describing total intensity, second-order central moments, and standardized skewness and kurtosis along the image axes. The CNN extractor instead receives the raw image, allowing relevant features to be learned directly from data.

The proposed architecture consists of four components: a resolution adapter, a convolutional feature extractor, a FiLM conditioning module, and a regression head. The resolution adapter resamples the input image to 256×256×3, as required by the EfficientNet-B0 backbone [13]; grayscale images are converted by channel replication. The classifier head of EfficientNet is removed so that the backbone outputs a 1280 × 8 × 8 feature map, which is compressed to 128 × 8 × 8 using a 1 × 1 convolution to preserve spatial information while reducing the feature dimension. Feature maps are conditioned using the prior vector p = [α, φs, log(Rref)]⊤, where α is the phase angle, φs the projected Sun direction in the image plane, and Rref the mean target radius. The logarithm compresses the dynamic range of possible values and is normalized to [0, 1] using fixed bounds. A small multilayer perceptron (MLP) maps p to channel-wise FiLM parameters (γ, β) ∈R128 that modulate the feature maps through affine transformations, initialized as the identity mapping (γ = 1, β = 0). The modulated feature maps are flattened and concatenated with cCOB and the bounding box features b before entering a shallow regression head with BatchNorm regularization [14]. The network predicts a normalized correction ∆ˆcCOB, yielding the final estimate ˆcCOF = cCOB +∆ˆcCOB. Image coordinates are normalized to [0, 1], improving numerical conditioning and removing dependence on image resolution.

Two additional centroiding algorithms are considered for comparison. ACOB applies a closed-form correction to the COB derived from a spherical photometric model. The prior vector is p = [α, φs, Rref, ρ]⊤, where ρ is the range to the COM. The apparent radius in pixels is computed as rref = arctan(Rref/ρ)/∆θ, where ∆θ is the camera instantaneous field of view in deg/px. Using the Lommel– Seeliger approximation [15], the corrected centroid is (1) ˆcCOF = cCOB + 0.0062 rref α◦ˆn where α◦is the phase angle in degrees and ˆn = [cos(φs + π), sin(φs + π)]⊤is the anti-Sun unit vector. NeuralCOB [11] replaces the analytical correction with a learned mapping from handcrafted features to the normalized COB correction. COB, bounding box, and brightness moments form a 17-dimensional feature vector processed by a four-layer MLP, composed of 10 754 parameters.

All datasets consist of grayscale synthetic images rendered using camera parameters representative of existing flight hardware, namely a resolution of 2048 × 1536 px and a FoV of 19.89◦× 14.98◦[8, 16]. These parameters yield a mean instantaneous field of view of ∆θ = 0.0097 deg/px = 35 arcsec/px which is used to convert centroiding errors expressed in pixels into line-of-sight angular errors expressed in degrees. The images are encoded at 8-bit depth (0–255 DN, uint8). Three subsets are used:

• Training set: Itokawa (50k), Bennu (50k), and Ceres (10k) samples. Image errors are introduced through runtime augmentations. An additional 15k samples for Itokawa and Bennu at closer distances are used during a second training stage (see Section 2.5).

• Validation set: Itokawa, Bennu, and Ceres (1000 samples each) with varying illumination and geometry conditions. Image errors are incorporated into the rendering process, including Poisson shot noise, Gaussian noise (1σ = 7 DN), and Gaussian blur.

• Evaluation set: Itokawa, Bennu, Mars, Moon, and Apophis (1000 samples each) with the same error sources used in the validation set. The validation and evaluation sets are rendered independently from the training set, with separate draws of camera pose and illumination and different random seeds, so that no sample is shared. The sampling distribution is nonetheless the same across all subsets and targets, which isolates the effect of the target shape from that of the observation geometry. Ceres is included only in the training set to increase morphological diversity. In fact, its nearly ellipsoidal shape introduces illumination patterns different from the highly irregular asteroids Itokawa and Bennu while also extending the range of body sizes seen during training. Although the COF is constrained to lie within the image plane, bodies may still appear partially outside the field of view, representing the most challenging condition. Range bounds are selected such that the apparent radius lies in [350, 768] px, corresponding to half the minimum image dimension; larger radii would saturate the field of view in nadir pointing, where the centroiding task becomes illposed. Camera positions are uniformly distributed within spherical caps defined by the range limits, while COF offsets in the image plane are generated by adding attitude errors. Similarly, phase angles are sampled uniformly in [0◦, 115◦], constraining the Sun positions in the scene. From these sets of poses, synthetic images are produced using an in-house ray-tracing renderer for small bodies and the ABRAM tool [17] for Mars and the Moon.

Extensive augmentations are applied during training to both images and prior inputs. Image augmentations include brightness and contrast variations, Gaussian noise, Gaussian blur, and “soft-binarize" (random blending between the image and its binarized version), together with horizontal and vertical flips. Prior inputs are perturbed with Gaussian errors with 1–σ of 2◦, 1◦, and 1% for phase angle, Sun direction, and reference radius, respectively, consistent with the knowledge accuracy expected during mission operations. These augmentations proved essential for improving robustness to input uncertainties. The FiLM and NeuralCOB models are trained in two stages using the AdamW optimizer [18]. In the first stage, the mean squared error loss is used with a plateau scheduler, stopping once the learning rate decreases below 10−7 from the initial value 5·10−3. Augmentation intensity is slightly reduced in this phase to facilitate convergence. In the second stage, the best checkpoints are fine-tuned using a Huber loss (δ = 0.65) and a cosine scheduler for 125 epochs. The final model is selected based on the validation loss.

The centroiding performance of ACOB, NeuralCOB, and the proposed FiLM-conditioned CNN is evaluated on the datasets described in Section 2.4. The analysis assesses both nominal accuracy and robustness to distribution shifts. Prior input errors follow the same distributions used during training (Section 2.5). The dependence of the centroiding error on observation geometry is analyzed through normalized range and phase angle. Errors are reported in pixels and, where relevant to the operational interpretation, converted into line-of-sight angles as specified in Section 2.4. Besides the three centroiding methods, an unconditioned variant of the proposed architecture, referred to as Plain CNN, is also evaluated. This is meant to provide the baseline performance that would be achievable from image features alone, in order to separate the contribution of the prior conditioning from that of the model capacity. The benefit of the selected prior features is then discussed.

Since both Itokawa and Bennu are included in the training set, this experiment represents the attainable performance when the network is trained on the actual targets shape. The resulting error distributions are shown in Figure 1. ACOB exhibits the largest spread of errors, while NeuralCOB substantially improves the results, reducing the mean error to 62.0 px and the median error to 46.4 px (corresponding to 0.60◦and 0.45◦). The FiLM model outperforms both, achieving a mean error of 24.3 px and a median error equal to 16.2 px (0.24◦and 0.16◦, respectively), while also reducing the number of large-error samples. For reference, the uncorrected COB is offset by 227.8 px (2.22◦) on average, about half the apparent radius, almost entirely along the anti-Sun direction. The learned correction reduces this systematic offset to a mean error vector of just 2.2 px, removing roughly 99% of the illuminationinduced bias, while the mean error norm drops by about 90%. Unlike ACOB and NeuralCOB, FiLM mainly fails only under particularly challenging scene conditions combined with very large off-pointing errors. The centroiding error depends on the observation geometry and is found to be correlated with the normalized range. Specifically, this quantity is inversely proportional to the apparent target size and therefore acts as a proxy for centroiding challenge. Smaller values correspond to larger apparent bodies, where the task becomes more ambiguous, particularly when the target is partially outside the field of view. In such cases the image alone may not be informative enough to infer the COF location. Across the entire interval of normalized distance and phase angles, FiLM consistently achieves the lowest errors and the tightest spread of samples. Neural- COB systematically lies between the analytical correction and the CNN model, a trend observed throughout the experiments.

blocks.html: To evaluate generalization capability, the same analysis was repeated on Apophis, which was not included in the training dataset either in terms of shape or prior distributions. Although the body is unseen during training, its morphology lies between that of Itokawa and Bennu. The resulting error distributions are shown in Figure 2. As expected, the absolute performance of all methods degrades compared to the previous experiment, yet remaining sufficient for navigation. The FiLM model attains a mean error of 73.9 px and a median of 62.2 px (0.72◦and 0.61◦), against 95.0 px (0.92◦) achieved by ACOB and 135.2 px (1.32◦) by NeuralCOB. At the distances considered in this evaluation, ranging from 1.4 to 2.7 km, the FiLM mean error corresponds to a cross-LoS position error of approximately 26 m. Nevertheless, FiLM still achieves the best performance across all statistics, although with a smaller advantage, while NeuralCOB fails to generalize and is outperformed by ACOB. This behavior can be explained by the limited representational power of the handcrafted features used by NeuralCOB and by the smaller capacity of the model compared to the CNN architecture. Note however that NeuralCOB serves a different purpose: rather than maximizing generalization like FiLM, it enables quick retuning and tailoring to a specific target when only limited training data are available, and is also more interpretable thanks to its small size and physically meaningful features. Note that ACOB requires range information, which may not always be readily available during operations, while learned models do not.

This experiment evaluates the algorithms on planetary bodies characterized by very different scales and surface properties compared to asteroids. The resulting error distributions are shown in Figure 3. The FiLM model again achieves the lowest errors, with mean 50.8 px and median 37.2 px. This result indicates that the model already generalizes well to nearly spherical targets despite the training set including only Ceres as representative of this class. In this scenario the ACOB model is no longer penalized by the non-spherical morphology typical of asteroids. Nevertheless, FiLM still achieves the best performance, suggesting that data-driven models can mitigate biases caused by partial visibility of the body. In fact, unlike the Apophis case, NeuralCOB also outperforms ACOB on this dataset. Overall, these results confirm that the learned approaches remain effective even when applied to bodies whose characteristics differ significantly from those present in the training set. Further fine-tuning on ellipsoidal targets would lead to additional improvements.

blocks.html: To better determine the contribution of the input priors conditioning in the observed performance improvement, the FiLM model is compared with the Plain CNN. This architecture shares the same backbone and regression head, only differing in the use of the prior knowledge through conditioning module and in the direct regression of the COF coordinates. The conditioning module accounts for 16 960 parameters (0.4% of the 4.2M total) so that the two models are effectively equivalent in capacity and computational cost. Despite these small differences, on the unseen datasets, the FiLM version reduces the mean error by 9% on Apophis and by 18.2% on Mars and the Moon, and the standard deviation by 10.3% and 22.3%, respectively. The improvement also extends to the tails of the distributions, with the 95th percentile reduced by 10.6% and 14.4% and the 99th percentile by 7.5% and 21.1%.

Although phase angle and Sun direction are in principle inferable from images, their estimation becomes ambiguous when the terminator is truncated due to close range or off-pointing, at very low phase angles, or for irregular bodies affected by self-shadowing. Providing these quantities as priors removes this ambiguity at negligible computational cost, since they are routinely available from Sun ephemerides and the spacecraft attitude estimate. On the other hand, the reference size addresses the monocular scale ambiguity, since target size and range cannot be separated from a single image. This makes Rref essential when a model is applied to targets spanning several orders of magnitude in size, as in the Mars and Moon experiments. Similarly, the COB anchor simplifies the learning task: instead of predicting the COF coordinates directly, the model estimates corrections to systematic COB error patterns that are strongly related to illumination conditions. The advantage with respect to the Plain CNN is therefore reasonably imputable to the enhanced generalization and regularization effect granted by the prior knowledge.

To complement the accuracy analysis, inference times were measured on a Jetson Orin Nano (8 GB, JetPack 6.2, 15 W mode). This platform is of interest as a candidate for future onboard computing in space applications [19]. The ONNX version of the models was used without optimization or quantization with the primary intent of highlighting the relative computational cost. Therefore, the results reported in Table 1 represent a conservative estimate for the networks. Notably, the FiLM model required about 52 ms for single image inference. Therefore, considering a reasonable image acquisition frequency of 5 minutes for close-proximity operations in deep space missions [20], the model appears to be compatible with onboard deployment.

blocks.html: This work evaluated a prior-informed convolutional model for the centroiding task and compared it with analytical and handcrafted-feature approaches across multiple targets and observation conditions. The results show that convolutional neural networks consistently outperform both analytical and handcrafted-feature methods, confirming their ability to capture the complex error patterns arising from irregular shapes and partial visibility.

Incorporating physical priors through FiLM conditioning further improves robustness and generalization, achieving the lowest errors and the tightest distributions across all evaluated targets. For completeness, the simpler Plain CNN directly regressing the centroid from the input image was also trained and evaluated under the same conditions. While it performed comparably on shapes present in the training data, its performance degraded significantly on unseen targets despite no significant difference in the model capacity. This indicates that the additional prior knowledge and conditioning module can enhance model generalization and regularize the model behaviour. Similarly, the COB provides a physically meaningful initial anchor and constrains the network to learn the residual correction. In terms of accuracy the advantage of the proposed model is substantial and consistent: across the three datasets FiLM reduces the mean centroiding error by 22 to 79% with respect to ACOB and by 31 to 61% with respect to NeuralCOB, up to a factor of 4.7 on the training shapes, and it is the best performing of the three methods on every target considered. Beyond the reduction in magnitude, the learned correction changes the nature of the error: the systematic anti-Sun bias of the raw COB is turned into a nearly zero-mean and isotropic residual, whose mean error vector is only 2.2 px on Itokawa and Bennu and 4.8 px on Apophis (5–7% of the corresponding RMS). This capability would significantly aid downstream state estimation algorithms, which are strongly impacted by systematic biases. Finally, it is worth noting that the methods are intentionally not equivalent in computational cost as the trade-off comparison among them is the focus of the analysis. ACOB and NeuralCOB are orders of magnitude cheaper and remain preferable when the onboard budget is severely constrained. The FiLM model sits at the opposite end of the trade-off, accepting a heavier backbone in exchange of accuracy gain and generalization to unseen targets. Several directions emerge for future work:

• The present evaluation relies on randomly sampled static scenes. Extending the analysis to realistic spacecraft trajectories would enable the study of temporal consistency, systematic biases, and edge cases.

• The inference benchmarks reported here are based on unoptimized ONNX models. Post-training quantization and hardware-specific optimizations are expected to significantly reduce latency and memory footprint.

• The prior-informed conditioning strategy explored for centroiding can be extended to other monocular navigation tasks, such as monocular range estimation where scale ambiguity may be resolved. Overall, these results indicate that combining physically motivated priors with data-driven models is a promising direction for improving the robustness of vision-based navigation algorithms.
